summary: Defines an authentication mechanism for the Port Control Protocol so a client can prove it is allowed to create, change or delete mappings on NATs or firewalls. This limits the security risk of uncontrolled mapping changes.

plainLanguage.summary: Before the doorman opens a hole in the fence for you, you must show your ID.

questions: how to secure port control protocol mappings
what is a pa session in pcp
how is the pcp transport key derived
subtitle: Lets a NAT or firewall check, using EAP, that a client is allowed to change its port mappings.

tldr.problem: The Port Control Protocol lets hosts create and delete mappings on NATs and firewalls, but uncontrolled changes are a security risk, and base PCP has no way to prove a client is authorized.
tldr.mechanism: The client and server run an EAP exchange carried inside PCP messages using a new AUTHENTICATION Opcode, derive a transport key from the resulting Master Session Key, and then tag every later PCP message with a MAC.
tldr.outcome: The server can check who a client is and what it may do before touching mappings, and every message in the session has integrity protection and origin authentication. The RFC updates RFC 6887.

today: RFC 7652 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 6887, the base PCP specification, by adding this authentication mechanism. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why PCP Needs Authentication
sections.content:
The Port Control Protocol (PCP, RFC 6887) lets an application manage address and port mappings on its NATs and firewalls. Because those devices matter for network security, there are many situations where unauthorized users must be kept out. This RFC adds a PCP security extension so that PCP servers can authenticate clients with the Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP). EAP messages travel inside PCP messages.

The design had to deal with lost EAP messages, reordered delivery, generation of transport keys, integrity protection and origin authentication for PCP messages, and algorithm agility. The RFC says it meets the Advanced Threat Model of base PCP. It names three places it can be used: security equipment such as corporate firewalls that create no implicit mappings, equipment such as Carrier-Grade NATs that serves several administrative domains, and any implementation that wants to be more permissive about letting applications create mappings for inbound traffic.

The PCP client acts as the EAP peer and the PCP server is integrated with an EAP authenticator. A PA session is the series of PCP exchanges between them, identified by a Session ID, and a PA Security Association (PCP SA) holds the shared keying material for it.
sections.plainLanguage: A gadget that opens gaps in a fence needs to know who is asking. This RFC gives it a way to ask for ID before it listens.

sections.title: Starting a Session
sections.content:
Every authentication message is a PCP message with the new AUTHENTICATION Opcode, whose Opcode-specific information is a Session ID and a Sequence Number. The session can start in two ways.

In client-triggered start, the client sends a PA-Initiation message with result code INITIATION, Session ID and Sequence Number set to zero, and a NONCE option holding a random nonce. If the server agrees, it answers with a PA-Server message carrying an EAP request and result code AUTHENTICATION_REQUEST. It MUST assign a unique Session ID and echo the nonce, which the client uses to check freshness.

In server-triggered start, the server rejects a common PCP request with an AUTHENTICATION_REQUIRED error and can send an unsolicited PA-Server message that begins the session. The client may answer, or silently discard it according to local policy.
sections.plainLanguage: Either you knock and say you want to talk, or the doorman tells you he needs ID before he does what you asked. Either way you get a ticket number for the visit.

sections.title: Running EAP Over PCP
sections.content:
An EAP request travels in a PA-Server message and an EAP response in a PA-Client message. Since EAP expects reliable delivery, a device sends nothing new until it gets a message with the proper sequence number from the other side. A device that cannot answer right away, for example while waiting for a user or for more fragments, MUST send a PA-Acknowledgement, which is a PA message with a RECEIVED_PAK option.

The EAP method MUST be a key-generating one. Implementations MUST support EAP-TTLS (RFC 5281) and SHOULD support TEAP (RFC 7170). A successful run yields a Master Session Key (MSK). In the first PA-Server message the server lists the pseudorandom functions (PRF options) and MAC algorithms (MAC_ALGORITHM options) it supports, and may add an ID_INDICATOR option to help the client pick the right credentials. The client picks one of each and returns them.

On success the server sends result code AUTHENTICATION_SUCCEEDED with a SESSION_LIFETIME option, protected by the new transport key. The first secure client message repeats the algorithm lists, and the server compares them with what it sent. If they differ it sends DOWNGRADE_ATTACK_DETECTED and ends the session. Failed authentication gives AUTHENTICATION_FAILED and failed authorization gives AUTHORIZATION_FAILED, and the session MUST end right after either.
sections.plainLanguage: The doorman and visitor swap ID checks in turns, and neither talks twice in a row. When it works, they agree on a secret signature style, and the doorman double-checks nobody tampered with the list of styles on offer.

sections.title: Recovery, Termination and Re-authentication
sections.content:
If a server loses its PCP SA, for example after a reboot, it sends an unsolicited ANNOUNCE response. Because that could be forged, the client sends an integrity-protected ANNOUNCE request. A success reply means an attacker sent the announcement. An UNKNOWN_SESSION_ID error means the state really is lost, and the client MUST run full EAP authentication again and then recreate its mappings. If the client loses its SA, the server rejects its unprotected requests with AUTHENTICATION_REQUIRED and the client MUST authenticate again.

Either side can end a session with result code SESSION_TERMINATED, and the other side responds the same way and removes its SA. A server MAY repeat a termination message up to ten times, with at least 250 ms between the first two and each later gap at least doubling.

A partner can re-authenticate to extend the lifetime without starting a new session. When the sequence number reaches 2^32 - 2^16, re-authentication MUST be triggered. Normal PCP messages may keep flowing under the current SA until the new one is ready, and sequence numbers reset to zero after success. If the session lifetime runs out without re-authentication, the session MUST be terminated.
sections.plainLanguage: If the doorman forgets everybody after a power cut, he asks for ID again. A visit can be ended politely by either side, and if your pass is about to expire you can renew it without leaving the building.

sections.title: The Security Association and Transport Key
sections.content:
Each side keeps a PCP SA for the life of the session. It holds the client and server addresses and UDP ports, the Session ID, four sequence numbers (next incoming and outgoing, for both PA messages and common PCP messages), the last outgoing message and retransmission interval, the MSK, the negotiated PRF and MAC algorithm, the transport key and its key ID, and the client's nonce.

The transport key is derived from the MSK as prf(MSK, "IETF PCP" || Session ID || Nonce || key ID), where || means concatenation. Its lifetime SHOULD match the session lifetime. A PCP implementation MUST support PRF_HMAC_SHA2_256 (transform ID 5) and AUTH_HMAC_SHA2_256_128 (transform ID 12).
sections.plainLanguage: After showing ID, both sides mix a shared secret with the visit ticket and some random numbers to make a special pen. Only they can sign with it.

sections.title: Message Format and Options
sections.content:
A PA-Server message uses the normal PCP response format. PA-Client messages use the PCP request header, but the Reserved byte now carries Opcode-specific data, which holds the result code. The Requested Lifetime and Lifetime fields are set to zero and ignored in PA messages.

The Opcode-specific information is a 32-bit Session ID and a 32-bit Sequence Number. The new options are:

  • NONCE: a random 32-bit number. A PA-Server message without the right nonce MUST be silently discarded.
  • AUTHENTICATION_TAG: for common PCP messages; carries Session ID, Sequence Number, Key ID and the MAC.
  • PA_AUTHENTICATION_TAG: for PA messages; carries just Key ID and the MAC, since the Opcode already has the rest.
  • EAP_PAYLOAD, PRF, MAC_ALGORITHM, SESSION_LIFETIME, RECEIVED_PAK and ID_INDICATOR, whose roles are described above.

The Key ID is filled with zeros if the MSK is used directly. The ID Indicator is a UTF-8 string that names the authority that issued the credentials, and the client compares it by exact octet-for-octet match.
sections.plainLanguage: Each note gets small stickers on it: a random number, the ticket number, a signature, or a piece of the ID check. Each sticker type has its own code number.

sections.title: Processing Rules
sections.content:
After EAP succeeds, every PCP message in the session MUST carry an authentication tag. To make one, the sender appends the tag option with the Authentication Data field set to zero, then computes a MAC over the entire message, including the header and the tag option, using the transport key, and writes the result into that field. A receiver finds the SA from the Session ID, sets the field aside, zeros it, recomputes the MAC and compares. Any mismatch, unknown SA or key, or bad sequence number means the message is silently discarded.

Retransmission follows Section 8.1.1 of RFC 6887, but here servers retransmit too. A retransmission MUST be bitwise identical to the original. Replies to duplicates MUST be rate limited to resist denial of service. If the maximum retransmission duration passes without a reply, the session ends and the SA is dropped.

PA messages must arrive with exactly the expected sequence number, which advances by 1 per new message. PA-Acknowledgement messages and retransmissions do not advance it. For common PCP messages, a message with a number smaller than the expected incoming value is rejected, which protects against replay. EAP methods handle MTU limits themselves; a long EAP message is split over several PA messages, with an acknowledgement for each.
sections.plainLanguage: Every note is signed over its whole text, so the doorman throws away any note that does not match its signature or that looks like an old copy.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Before a transport key exists, PA messages have little cryptographic protection. The first PA-Server and PA-Client exchange can be spoofed if no secure channel is already in place, and is open to man-in-the-middle and denial-of-service attacks. Because the PRF and MAC lists are sent at this stage, an attacker might strip the strong algorithms and push the client toward the weakest, so the server needs to offer only strong algorithms. The later comparison of algorithm lists is what detects this.

To limit denial of service, a device SHOULD create as little state as possible in the first exchanges. The EAP method must resist attacks in an insecure network, provide user-identity confidentiality and protection against dictionary attacks, and support session-key establishment. A PCP proxy placed between clients and a server may authenticate to the server itself, and its re-authentication does not interrupt the service it gives to clients.
sections.plainLanguage: At the very start, before the secret pen exists, a trickster could mess with the conversation. So the doorman keeps almost no notes at first and only accepts strong signing styles.

fields.name: Sequence Number
fields.desc: A 32-bit number incremented on every new, non-retransmitted outgoing PA message.

viz.caption: PCP RESULT CODES ALLOCATED BY THE RFC

items.label: INITIATION
items.desc: Client asks the server to start authentication.

items.label: AUTHORIZATION_FAILED
items.desc: Error: authentication worked but authorization failed.

items.label: SESSION_TERMINATED
items.desc: The PA session must be terminated.

items.label: UNKNOWN_SESSION_ID
items.desc: No known PA session for the Session ID sent.

items.label: DOWNGRADE_ATTACK_DETECTED
items.desc: Server detected an algorithm downgrade attack.

items.label: AUTHENTICATION_REQUEST
items.desc: The PA message contains an EAP request.

items.label: AUTHENTICATION_REPLY
items.desc: The PA message contains an EAP response.

viz.caption: PCP OPTION CODES DEFINED BY THE RFC

items.label: NONCE
items.desc: Random 32-bit number to check message freshness.

items.label: AUTHENTICATION_TAG
items.desc: MAC and session fields for common PCP messages.

items.label: PRF
items.desc: A pseudorandom function the sender supports.

items.label: MAC_ALGORITHM
items.desc: A MAC algorithm the sender supports.

items.label: SESSION_LIFETIME
items.desc: Lifetime of the PA session in seconds.

items.label: RECEIVED_PAK
items.desc: Acknowledges receipt of a PA message.

items.label: ID_INDICATOR
items.desc: Names the authority that issued the credentials to use.
